newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Jurong Shipyard profits dip, repairs up.
newsitem.headline: Jurong Shipyard profits dip, repairs up.

text.p: Jurong Shipyard Ltd said on Saturday its net profit dropped 18 percent in the year ended December 1996 to Singapore $31.7 million (US$22 million). But company officials said ship repair jobs rose by 19 percent.
The group's revenue rose 10 percent to S$357.2 million while the yard saw a 14 percent profit slash to S$25.56 million and a two percent profit drop to S$301.86 million.
The company said in a statement it was affected by the depressed ship repair market but expected to remain profitable in 1997.
According to Edinburgh Financial Publication's Estimate Directory, Jurong's net profit was expected to be around S$32 million.
Despite the gloom in the industry, Jurong's number of repair jobs rose to 235 vessels in 1996 from 198 in 1995, a 19 percent increase, chairman Lua Cheng Eng told a news conference.
Of the 235 vessels, 52 percent were tankers, comprising 16 Very-Large Crude Carriers (VLCC) and 10 Ultra-Large Crude Carriers (ULCC), he said.

In 1995, the company was able to accept only 11 VLCCs before expanding its docks. Jurong opened its new 400,000 deadweight tonnes (dwt) drydock last July. The new docks added about S$32 million last year and were expected to generate more this year.
"We are forecasting S$70-80 million in revenue from the new docks this year," Lua said.
Despite receiving more repair jobs in 1996, Jurong saw the average repair value per ship decline 13 percent to S$940,000 from S$1.08 million in 1995, managing director Tan Kwi Kin said.
Tan said he did not see a significant change in the repair market conditions but hoped Jurong's new docks would enable the company to clinch jobs from VLCCs and ULCCs.
Jurong also intended to capture more repair and upgrading jobs from off-shore floating structures, Tan said.
"We already have quite a number of ships that would cushion the depressed ship repair market," Tan said. Jurong aimed to achieve S$100 million in contributions from these jobs in 1997, he added.
Jurong expected a busy year of shipbuilding with seven vessels in hand, worth a total of S$220 million, Tan said.
Company officials said Jurong would continue to concentrate on its core business of ship repair despite the prevailing weak margins of 5-6 percent.

Analysts said they would call a hold on Jurong shares at S$6.40, the level it ended at on Friday. But many were wary about the company's prospects given Sembawang Corp takeover proposal last November.
In the proposed merger, SembCorp is to inject S$279.28 million of its shipyard and engineering assets into Jurong in return for 41.07 million new Jurong shares at S$6.80 each.

"Jurong is fine without the merger clouding its prospect," said one analyst with a local brokerage house. "There is so much uncertainty as to whether the merger will take place. If it does, it will be negative for Jurong."

Concerns over the potential merger was exacerbated when Jurong shares fell below SembCorp's S$6.80 takeover offer price. "It shows people don't like the deal and are worried whether it will go through," another analyst said.
"I say buy the stock at currrent levels if you are betting the merger will go through," said the analyst at a local brokerage house.
-- Singapore newsroom (65 86030830)
